1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text:
Introduction: Although cough appears to be a very common symptom, in this middle-aged woman it triggered a complex and prolonged medical workup. Over the past 2 years, this patient had been suffering from recurrent cough. Imaging showed patchy increased-density opacities in the right lower lung and near the hilum, but both antibacterial and anti-TB treatments were ineffective, causing the diagnosis to repeatedly reach an impasse.
Basic information: Female patient, 59 years old, from Yantai, Shandong, was admitted to our Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough for 2 years, pulmonary shadow found for 1.5 years."
History of present illness: In approximately 27 months before Day 0, the patient developed "recurrent cough" immediately after routine vaccination, and subsequently took traditional Chinese medicine for 1 year without improvement. On Day -461, she presented to a Class A hospital in Yantai, where chest CT showed bilateral lung infection (more prominent in the right lung). She was treated with cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam for anti-infective therapy, but there was no significant improvement in either symptoms or imaging. After discharge, she continued long-term traditional Chinese medicine treatment, but the cough remained recurrent. On Day -148, she presented to another hospital in Yantai, where chest CT showed a large area of increased density in the right lower lobe with no significant change compared with before. Endobronchial ultrasound bronchoscopy showed a lesion in the lateral basal segment of the right lower lobe. TBNA pathology showed fibroblast proliferation in the alveolar septa, and no definite tumor cells were identified. She subsequently received levofloxacin and cefmetazole sodium for anti-infective therapy combined with steroids for anti-inflammatory treatment, but neither symptoms nor imaging improved significantly. Empiric anti-TB therapy was then given, after which the patient developed adverse reactions including dizziness, nausea, and vertigo, so anti-TB treatment was discontinued. On Day -102, she presented to a hospital in Shandong and underwent PET-CT, which showed: "1. Right lung soft tissue lesion with partially increased metabolism; percutaneous biopsy is recommended to exclude primary pulmonary lymphoma of inflammatory type; 2. Multiple small mediastinal lymph nodes with partially increased metabolism; regular follow-up is recommended; 3. Tiny bilateral pulmonary nodules, with no abnormal metabolism; 4. Postoperative changes of the thyroid." On Day -99, she presented to a hospital in Beijing, where needle biopsy of the right lower lung consolidation lesion was performed. Pathology showed "chronic inflammation in submitted fibrous tissue, with focal lymphocyte aggregation," with no evidence of tumor. At that time, she was treated with roxithromycin and KeKe tablets, and the cough was slightly relieved. On Day -76, she again visited the outpatient clinic of another hospital in Beijing and was given ertapenem for anti-infective therapy, with slight symptom relief. Chest CT on Day -70 showed "multiple patchy and faint patchy indistinct opacities near the right hilum and paraspinal region, with partial consolidation, more severe in the lower lobe, infection considered more likely; multiple tiny nodules in both lungs; small mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, some calcified." After nearly 1 month of ertapenem anti-infective therapy, she returned to that hospital for follow-up on Day -36. Repeat chest CT showed "multiple patchy and faint patchy indistinct opacities near the right hilum and paraspinal region, slightly more extensive than before." Diagnostic anti-TB therapy was prescribed in the outpatient setting: oral isoniazid, ethambutol, linezolid, clarithromycin, and moxifloxacin. After taking the medications, the patient developed fatigue and discomfort, and symptoms did not improve significantly. On Day -21, she developed fever without an obvious precipitating factor, with a maximum temperature of 38.2℃, accompanied by worsening cough and white sputum. The fever improved after oral acetaminophen that day. She presented to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid testing was negative, and was treated with cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam + dexamethasone + levofloxacin. Her temperature normalized, but the cough still did not improve. On Day -8, she again presented to the same hospital in Beijing. Chest CT was basically unchanged from before. Empiric anti-TB therapy was again given and has been continued to date: isoniazid 0.3 qd, ethambutol 0.45 qd, linezolid 0.6 qd.
Past medical history: The patient is usually in fair general health. She denies a history of "hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or coronary artery disease," and denies a history of infectious diseases such as "hepatitis or TB." In 2003 and 2022, she underwent surgery twice for "benign thyroid nodules." After surgery, she took Euthyrox orally, and follow-up thyroid-related indices showed no obvious abnormalities.
Personal and family history: The patient was born in her native place. She has no history of exposure to dust, toxic substances, or radioactive materials; no history of contact with epidemic areas; no smoking or alcohol use; married at the appropriate age; her spouse and one son are both healthy; she denies a family history of hereditary disease.
Physical examination: T 36.5℃, P 80 beats/min, R 20 breaths/min, BP 120/70 mmHg. Clear consciousness. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body. Moist rales and wheezing were heard in both lungs, more obvious in the right lung than the left. Cardiac dullness was not enlarged. Heart rate 80 beats/min, regular rhythm, no pathologic murmurs heard in any valvular auscultation area. Abdomen flat and soft, no tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable below the costal margin, no edema in either lower extremity. Bilateral pathologic signs negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary pulmonary lymphoma (represented by MALT lymphoma)
supporting_evidence: The disease course has lasted for 2 years, characterized by persistent/recurrent cough and persistent pulmonary opacities, consistent with the feature that indolent lymphoproliferative disorders can have a prolonged course.

After multiple courses of antibacterial therapy, steroid anti-inflammatory therapy, and empiric anti-TB treatment, there was no significant improvement in symptoms or imaging findings, which does not support a common infectious lesion.
PET-CT showed “a right lung soft tissue lesion with partially increased metabolic activity; puncture biopsy is recommended to rule out inflammatory primary pulmonary lymphoma”

Needle biopsy pathology suggested "chronic inflammation in the submitted fibrous tissue, with focal lymphocytic aggregation," and TBNA pathology suggested "fibroblastic proliferation in the alveolar septa," which may be seen in lymphoproliferative lesions with insufficient sampling or in a peripheral inflammatory reaction.

Chest CT and the accompanying images show that the lesions are predominantly persistent patchy opacities/consolidation in the right lower lung and perihilar region, with localized delayed non-absorption, consistent with the fact that pulmonary lymphoma may present as focal consolidation or mass-like opacities.
Small mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes are present, with increased metabolism in some, increasing the possibility of lymphatic system disease
opposing_evidence: Neither of the two pathology examinations showed definite tumor cells, and no direct pathological evidence of lymphoma was obtained.
Physical examination showed no enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body, with no obvious manifestations of systemic lymphatic system involvement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung / pneumonic-type lung adenocarcinoma
supporting_evidence: Persistent large patchy area of increased density/consolidation in the right lower lung and near the hilum, with essentially no absorption for more than 1.5 years, and some follow-up examinations suggesting a slightly larger extent, consistent with the presentation of pneumonic-type adenocarcinoma as prolonged consolidation
After treatment with multiple antimicrobial agents, there was no significant improvement in either imaging findings or symptoms, which does not support simple infection alone.
PET-CT showed a right lung soft tissue lesion with partially increased metabolic activity, suggesting that a neoplastic lesion cannot be excluded

The attached CT images show a focal persistent area of consolidation near the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, with a unilateral predominant distribution, consistent with one of the imaging warning features of lung cancer, especially pneumonic-type adenocarcinoma.
Cough is the main symptom, recently accompanied by white sputum; this may be seen in mucinous adenocarcinoma
opposing_evidence: No evidence of tumor was found on either EBUS-TBNA or percutaneous needle biopsy.
The lesion has been present for a long time, but PET shows only "partially increased metabolic activity"; the metabolic activity is not very intense.
The phase 1 information did not provide typical malignancy-related manifestations, such as significant weight loss, hemoptysis, or progressively worsening general condition.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (cryptogenic or secondary)
supporting_evidence: Persistent cough; repeated chest CT showed multiple patchy and faint ill-defined opacities in the right lung near the hilum and paraspinal region, with partial consolidation, more severe in the lower lobe; the imaging pattern can be seen in organizing pneumonia
TBNA pathology suggested “fibroblast proliferation in the alveolar septa,” consistent with fibrosis/reparative changes in an organizing lesion
Percutaneous needle biopsy suggested “chronic inflammation, with focal lymphocytic aggregation,” which may be consistent with a chronic inflammatory/organizing lesion.
On physical examination, wet rales and wheezing were heard in both lungs, more prominent on the right, supporting inflammatory involvement of the airways and lung parenchyma
On imaging, the lesions are persistent, partially fluctuating, and slightly progressive; this can be seen in organizing pneumonia.
opposing_evidence: After combined corticosteroid anti-inflammatory therapy, neither the symptoms nor the imaging findings showed significant improvement, which is inconsistent with the fact that typical organizing pneumonia often responds well to glucocorticoids.
The lesion has long been confined to the right lower lung and the perihilar region, with a very prolonged duration; compared with typical organizing pneumonia, it is more focal and refractory.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
supporting_evidence: Chronic cough with a long disease course and recent fever is a common manifestation of chronic infectious disease.
Persistent right lung-predominant pulmonary opacities; mycobacterial infection should be considered when there is no response to conventional antibacterial therapy

The chest CT report mentions multiple micronodular opacities in both lungs and small mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, some calcified, all of which can be seen in prior or chronic mycobacterial-related changes.
Multiple hospitals repeatedly considered TB clinically and administered empiric anti-TB treatment, indicating that TB was clinically suspected to some extent in the first-stage data
opposing_evidence: After empiric anti-TB treatment, symptoms showed no significant relief, and imaging showed no significant improvement.
Pathology did not indicate evidence supporting TB, such as granulomatous inflammation or caseous necrosis.
The attached imaging mainly shows persistent consolidation/patchy opacities in the right lower lung and near the hilar region, which are not typical manifestations of TB

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic fungal lung infection
supporting_evidence: Prolonged disease course; both antibacterial therapy and empiric anti-TB therapy have had no obvious effect, and infection with uncommon pathogens should be considered.

Despite recent corticosteroid anti-inflammatory treatment, there was still no improvement, and subsequently fever and worsening cough developed; chronic fungal infection should be included in the differential diagnosis.
Chest CT and the accompanying images show persistent focal consolidation/patchy opacity in the right lower lung, which can be seen as a nonspecific manifestation of some chronic fungal infections
Needle biopsy pathology showed only chronic inflammation and lymphocytic aggregation; an infectious lesion cannot be excluded if the sampling missed the pathogen.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, no underlying immunosuppressive disease, history of long-term corticosteroid use, or definite history of fungal exposure was provided.
No characteristic pathological features related to fungal infection were identified.
First-stage imaging did not show findings more supportive of fungal infection, such as typical cavitation, a fungus ball, or the halo sign.

recommended_exams.exam: BALF cytology
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [BALF cytology]: A small number of atypical cell clusters are seen; please submit specimens for examination multiple times.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent cough for 2 years, and a long-standing nonresolving area of consolidation in the right lower lung and near the hilar region. Anti-infective therapy, corticosteroids, and empiric anti-TB treatment were all ineffective, suggesting that a simple infection is unlikely and that a neoplastic lesion should be a major consideration. Previous BALF cell block preparation failed, and repeated EBUS aspiration cytology was inconclusive; however, the current BALF cytology has shown a small number of atypical cell clusters, indicating that the airway specimen may already be close to the nature of the lesion. Continuing BALF cytology with multiple submissions is intended to increase the detection rate of abnormal cells and, as much as possible, obtain malignant cytologic evidence with a less traumatic approach, to help determine whether this is a glandular epithelial tumor such as pneumonic-type/invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, while differentiating it from chronic inflammation, organizing pneumonia, and some infectious lesions, and to provide a basis for whether more invasive tissue sampling and treatment decisions will be needed subsequently.

recommended_exams.exam: Histopathologic examination of needle biopsy tissue from the primary lesion of the right lung
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [Needle biopsy tissue from the primary lesion of the right lung] Our hospital: a small amount of fragmented mucosal epithelium and cell debris-like material, predominantly mucinous epithelium, with mild atypia. Two possibilities are considered: bronchial adenoma with atypical hyperplasia or well-differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma. The cells observable in the biopsy tissue are limited; definitive diagnosis is pending further evaluation of the surgical resection specimen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had a prolonged disease course, with imaging persistently showing focal consolidation in the right lung and slight progression at one point, and multiple courses of anti-infective and anti-TB treatment have been ineffective; clinically, the central question of "chronic inflammation or tumor" must be resolved. Multiple prior TBNA procedures and percutaneous biopsies failed to establish a definitive diagnosis, but biopsy tissue from the primary lesion in the right lung this time has already shown predominantly mucinous epithelium, suggesting that the lesion may have evolved from an inflammatory lesion to bronchial adenoma with atypical hyperplasia or well-differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma. Histopathologic examination must be performed because it can directly assess tumor architecture, pattern of invasion, and mucin secretion characteristics; it is the key basis for distinguishing benign from malignant lesions, differentiating mucinous adenocarcinoma from reactive mucosal epithelial changes, and excluding nonepithelial lesions such as lymphoma and organizing pneumonia, and it also determines whether surgical resection rather than continued empiric medical treatment should be pursued next.

recommended_exams.exam: Immunohistochemistry of needle biopsy tissue from the primary lesion in the right lung
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry: 1 (slide no.): TTF-1 (negative in most glandular epithelial cells, few positive), Napsin A (-), CK7 (+), P53 (weak+), Ki-67 (occasional individual epithelial cells+), P40 (-), CK20 (-), Villin (weak+), CDX-2 (-), P63 (occasional individual positive cells).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the setting of a prolonged clinical course and imaging findings resembling inflammatory-type lesions, morphology based on only a small amount of needle biopsy tissue is insufficient to reliably distinguish well-differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma, bronchiolar adenoma-like lesions, and reactive mucinous epithelial hyperplasia. Performing immunohistochemistry on the primary lesion is intended to further clarify the epithelial lineage and direction of differentiation of the lesion: CK7 supports pulmonary glandular epithelial origin; P40/P63 are essentially negative, arguing against squamous differentiation; negative or low expression of TTF-1 and Napsin A, although atypical, can be seen in pulmonary invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma; meanwhile, CK20, CDX-2, and Villin are helpful in assessing the differential issue of possible metastatic disease from a gastrointestinal primary. This evaluation can increase diagnostic confidence when tissue is limited and morphologic atypia is not prominent, helping determine whether the lesion is primary pulmonary mucinous adenocarcinoma or adenocarcinoma from another origin/non-neoplastic lesion, and providing important support for surgery and subsequent pathologic classification.

recommended_exams.exam: Pathologic examination of a surgical gross specimen
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The biopsy tissue contains a limited number of observable cells; further clarification of the diagnosis awaits the larger surgical specimen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had a persistent right lung lesion for 2 years, with long-term non-resolution and recent fluctuations including worsening cough and fever. Although multiple infectious disease tests were negative and pathology gradually suggested the possibility of adenocarcinoma, all earlier small-specimen samples had problems of insufficient sampling, low cellularity, and non-typical atypia. Pathologic examination of the surgical large specimen can provide information on the full extent of the lesion, depth of invasion, mucinous component, spread through air spaces, bronchial and pleural involvement, margin status, and lymph node status, and is the gold standard for the definitive diagnosis of invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung and completion of staging assessment. This examination is used not only to resolve the problem that 'small specimens cannot establish a definitive characterization,' but also directly relates to whether further postoperative treatment is needed, prognosis assessment, and formulation of a follow-up plan.

recommended_exams.exam: Pathologic examination of submucosal soft tissue from the orifice of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [Submucosal soft tissue at the orifice of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe] sent out: adenocarcinoma (note: favor mucinous adenocarcinoma).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Bronchoscopy has revealed a submucosal soft tissue lesion at the opening of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe, with mild local luminal stenosis, which is anatomically consistent with the patient's longstanding focal right lower lung lesion. Previous BALF culture, acid-fast staining, mycologic studies, and inflammatory markers did not support active infection, whereas the pathology of the submucosal soft tissue at this site has directly suggested adenocarcinoma, favoring mucinous adenocarcinoma. Therefore, the purpose of performing a pathologic examination of this site is to obtain representative tissue from a location closer to the airway lesion, in order to verify whether this persistent consolidation is essentially airway-related adenocarcinoma rather than inflammatory granuloma, organizing lesion, or lymphoproliferative lesion. This examination can compensate for the limitations of repeatedly negative percutaneous biopsy and cytology, help establish definitive malignant pathologic evidence, and provide a basis for planning the extent of subsequent surgical resection.

recommended_exams.exam: Immunohistochemistry of the submucosal soft tissue at the orifice of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry results: paraffin block No. 1: CKpan (+), CEA (-), TTF-1 (-), Napsin A (-), Ki-67 (+, 5%), EGFR (-), P53 (+)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the pathology of the submucosal soft tissue of the bronchial mucosa had already favored adenocarcinoma in this patient, because the lesion had long clinically resembled infection, and mucinous adenocarcinoma often shows low metabolic activity, low atypia, and negative routine tumor markers, morphology alone could still be confused with a benign mucinous lesion or metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry of this site was performed to further confirm the epithelial neoplastic nature of the lesion and help determine its origin: CKpan positivity supports an epithelial origin; negative TTF-1/Napsin A, although atypical, can be consistent with pulmonary invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma; a low Ki-67 suggests relatively slow tumor proliferation, which is also consistent with its protracted clinical course; and positive P53 supports a neoplastic change. This examination helps correlate the pathology of the localized airway lesion with that of the primary lesion, improves diagnostic concordance, and provides a pathologic basis for determining surgery rather than continuing anti-infective treatment.

recommended_exams.exam: Gomori methenamine silver stain
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had a long disease course and previously received corticosteroids and multiple courses of anti-infective therapy. mNGS of tissue obtained by EBUS aspiration had also detected a small number of Rhizopus, although the sequence count was very low and the clinical presentation was not typical; however, chronic fungal infection did indeed need to be excluded in the initial differential diagnosis. Gomori methenamine silver stain is an important special stain in histopathology for identifying fungal components and can directly determine whether fungal hyphae are present, thereby helping determine whether the lesion is infectious or neoplastic. The clinical question for this test in this case was to exclude fungal infection, especially invasive fungal infection, as the cause of the submucosal soft tissue or consolidation opacity, so as to avoid misdiagnosing infection as a tumor and proceeding rashly to surgery. The result was negative. Combined with a negative G test, negative fungal culture, and an overall disease course inconsistent with the rapid progression characteristic of mucormycosis, this helps reduce the likelihood of fungal pneumonia and supports focusing the diagnostic direction on mucinous adenocarcinoma.

treatment_plan: Thoracoscopic right middle and lower lobectomy
Postoperatively, the patient was treated with fluid replacement, infection prophylaxis, hemostasis, nebulization, and expectorant therapy.
treatment_response: The procedure was uneventful, the general postoperative condition was acceptable, and the patient was discharged on Day +23.
